Introduction
The Promoting Electric Propulsion (PEP) competition provides a platform for students
from different universities to come together and prove the autonomous capabilities of their
electric motorboats. This year, our team focused on expanding the autonomous capabilities of
our boat by improving the navigation and computer vision. Our team also expanded our
telemetry and simulation capabilities to better validate our software. Our goal with this software
is to make it adaptable to any type of marine vehicle.

                                      Introduction
        The Promoting Electric Propulsion (PEP) competition provides a platform for students
from different universities to come together and prove the autonomous capabilities of their
electric motorboats. This year, our team focused on expanding the autonomous capabilities of
our boat by improving the navigation and computer vision. Our team also expanded our
telemetry and simulation capabilities to better validate our software. Our goal with this software
is to make it adaptable to any type of marine vehicle.

Autoboat at Virginia Tech

Background Information
Problem Statement
Gasoline and diesel engines have seen sufficient widespread use in both recreational
and commercial naval vessels to the point where environmental factors must be considered[1].
While this is certainly not a new finding, there remains a steady research effort into alternative
propulsion methods. One such alternative is the use of electric motors powered by new
advances in battery technology, which promise to reduce waste, increase efficiency, and
operate quieter compared to their combustion counterparts[2]. Many other sectors are embracing
electrification, such as in the electric car market, where in the U.S., 1.4 million new electric
vehicles were registered in 2023 alone, and ever since then, adoption has been quickly
accelerating[3]. To prove the efficacy of electric engines, our team’s goal was to create a
two-meter, remote controlled and autonomous, electric propulsion boat that both maximizes
battery life and speed for the hull size.
In addition to electric propulsion, there are also broader efforts to expand the capabilities
of unmanned autonomous boats. For example, in the last two years, Saronic has invested $300
million dollars towards growing the Louisiana Bayou economy by developing autonomous
surface vessels. This effort plans to create 1,500 direct new jobs with an average annual salary
of $87,936 at full employment, demonstrating that there is a market for this kind of technology[4].
As a result of these interests, AutoBoat at VT aims to expand upon autopilot technology.

PEP at Virginia Tech
The Virginia Tech PEP team is located on campus in the Joe F. Ware Lab. Our team
draws from a wide range of engineering disciplines, including Ocean, Aerospace, Mechanical,
Computer Engineering, Electrical Engineering, and Computer/Data Science, to foster a highly
interdisciplinary environment where subteams share their expertise at every step of the problem
design. With around 40 active members, our involvement in PEP creates a collaborative and
hands-on environment where students gain experience working on complex engineering
systems. Members are involved in all stages of the process, from initial concept designs to final
testing.

Figure 1. Left: Autoboat team leads. Right: Entire team.

Displacement Hull Conversion
Theseus was originally built for the International SailBot competition, competing several
years before its conversion to a motorboat in 2025. The structure was designed to operate with
a 20 lb keel. The keel was removed to reduce weight to allow for the addition of motorization
components. This freed 30 lbs of payload and system mass, but also reduced the stability and
maneuverability of the boat.

Figure 2. Left: On the water test of Theseus before the 2023 SailBot Competition. Right:
Theseus during testing in Fall 2024 after conversion.
The original structure was not designed to easily reach planing. Therefore, a stepped
section was added at the stern. The addition of the steep section changed the hull shape to a
deep planing hull, instead of the gentle slope seen in the original design. The deep-planing hull
generates greater values of hydrodynamic lift, which in turn reduces the wetted surface area. A
smaller wetted surface area decreases the amount of drag over the bottom of the hull. It also
allows for the boat to cut more easily through the water, have greater stability at speed, and cut
through waves more easily. The addition of the chine strip also allows for a tighter turning
radius.
At the end of last year, the boat was experiencing a significant heel when turning in one
direction. This indicated an imbalance in either the weight or hydrodynamic forces. Over the
past year, the naval architecture team has been focused on identifying and addressing the
principal causes of this behavior. This included investigating the weight distribution of the
structure and systems to improve balance and stability. It also included minimizing the surface
discontinuities and imperfections along the hull. By smoothing the hull and reducing
irregularities, we aimed to decrease drag and ensure more uniform flow over the surface, which
would ultimately reduce the effect of the forces causing the heel.
The first iteration of our conversion contained rounded, semi-circular, wooden strakes.
Throughout the past two years, the team has had a goal of creating strakes with the ability to
improve our speed, maneuverability, and stability, while also hoping to reduce their weight. Last
year, we went through the steps of examining three different shapes: trapezoidal, triangular, and
semi-circular. Finally, we examined the semi-circular strakes. This option allowed us to maintain
our current maneuverability; however, they generate very little lift across the hull and delays
planing.
Over the past year, we have implemented our new strake design. We settled on the
triangular strakes to decrease drag and increase maneuverability in the water. The strakes were

Rudders and Stuffing Boxes
For our rudders, the team chose a four-bar linkage because they have a tunable
mechanical advantage. The linkage also ensures the rudders stay parallel. A gear train was
attempted in the past, but proved to be hard to maintain and adjust. The linkage bars were
made with several holes so the coupler rod can be moved around to get more or less
mechanical advantage (MA) in exchange for more/less output arc.

Figure 5. Four-Bar linkage in action

Figure 6. Mechanical advantage calculations for Linkage
The graph on the left is the overall MA for 0-180 deg input. Note that the MA approaches
infinity on either side of ~36 deg. The location changes when the lengths of the bars change, but
there will always be this discontinuity. The MA has been clamped at 7, so the graphs are visible.
The graph on the right is a zoomed-in version of the left graph; it shows the 45-degree angle on
either side of the output center of rotation. The output CoR is the state where the output
(rudders) are in the middle of their arc. This is NOT the center of the input arc. The dotted line is
the mirrored MA, which helps show symmetry in the MA for starboard vs port turns. If the MA is
too asymmetrical, we might run into issues where the motor skips, but only for right turns.
To prevent water from coming through the rudder holes, we implemented scaled-down
versions of a traditional stuffing box. Our box is made of two brass pipe fittings that thread down
on each other, compressing the stuffing against the shaft. This allows the shaft to rotate while
preventing water from entering the boat.
In our case, we had to make an additional piece that we call the compression ring. It gets
pushed down into the lower portion of the box and compresses the stuffing. It’s also worth
noting that this can be done far more efficiently if you make your own fittings.

High-Level System Design
        This year, we have set a multitude of difficult objectives in electrical design and firmware
alike. The primary objective was the implementation of a higher degree of firmware modularity
through the use of C++. We have chosen to break away from our older implementation in C to
implement an object-oriented programming paradigm. We have decided against switching over



                                                                                                   7

pages.text:
Autoboat at Virginia Tech
to the declarative programming paradigm as provided by the standard library due to our natural
affinity for low-level algorithms that high-level abstractions would obscure rather than simplify.
Electronically, we have taken a similar philosophy to break down our system into testable
components that are easy to fix if broken.
For our firmware system, we utilize a cheap bare metal microcontroller by the name of
RP2040, stationed on the Raspberry Pi Pico. It would interact with Jetson Orin Nano, our
computer vision and autonomy board. They interact through a USB interface using the ROS2
middleware environment. Raspberry Pi Pico controls all of our low-level peripherals connected
over I2C, SPI, and UART. This configuration ensures that our peripherals work independently of
the current Jetson model that we use, as well as protects our more expensive electronics from
miswiring and overvolting. If we accidentally overvolt our RP2040, it only costs $5 to replace,
but if we overvolt the Jetson, then it would take a few hundred dollars out of our budget.
Therefore, the only connection between the Jetson and the electrical system is an optically
isolated USB cable in order to protect it.
Our PCBs were designed with the same idea in mind though for slightly different
reasons. Last year, we ran into a problem where our power distribution system would break far
more often than our low-level logic, but it would take the latter with it due to them being located
on the same PCB. We would have to disassemble our entire system should we find ourselves in
the need to debug an interface, solder a faulty component, or screw in a loose terminal. This is
not a good practice and we now step away from it. We have split our old master PCB into the
smaller digital portion and the larger analog portion. The analog portion is equipped with custom
buck converter modules tailored to our larger system for efficiency. You can find the detailed
discussion of both below.

Firmware and MicroROS
In order for the electrical systems to function properly, effective communication between
components is vital. We utilized the MicroROS open source framework to create a
communication network between our software system and sensor suite. MicroROS allows the
microcontrollers to use the same framework as ROS2. Within the context of the Jetson and
overall system, the MicroROS framework running on the Pi Pico can be considered as one
node. One goal this year was for the MicroROS architecture to be applicable to multiple
autonomous vehicles, so the node itself has to be well organized internally, as its role within the
system and the sensors it manages change depending on the vehicle.
To accomplish this goal, we refactored our original MicroROS C Code into C++ to
enhance readability and make the code more modular. On one side of the architecture is
hardware communication. The peripherals are split into their communication protocols (I2C, SPI,
UART). This standardizes the write/read byte functions between all embedded sensors, making
the libraries much more modular and increasing the ease of adding future sensors for future
years. Each device-specific class then inherits from the communication base class. The relevant
functions that need to be exposed to the higher-level architecture are done so via the HAL
namespace.

On the other side of the architecture is the MicroROS class. This specifically handles
spinning up all the relevant topics and the related messages. Each peripheral is a node in the
MicroROS structure and is represented with a struct to compartmentalize all relevant
information. The System class then integrates the HAL and MicroROS classes and initializes
and runs the entire application. By separating the hardware communication from the MicroROS,
we are able to better identify and debug issues. A graphical representation is provided below.

Figure 9. number
In addition, we are also working on an interrupt-based system for our embedded sensor
suite and its publishing to its respective topics. Since waiting for protocols like I2C to complete
can block the rest of the program, there's a risk that it can degrade the performance of the boat
and create issues. To counteract this, we started designing a new framework that sends the
transmitted data, continues the rest of the code, and triggers an interrupt that handles the
received data at the moment it has finished arriving. Although the system has not been
completed by this competition, it would help create a much more robust system and mitigate risk
in the future

pages.text:
Autoboat at Virginia Tech
Our Digital Communication is handled by our PCB. It contains pins for a Raspberry Pi
Pico, two DRV8711 motor controllers, a relay for our contactor, status LEDs for our signals, a
chip select multiplexer, output pins to connect with sensors, and debug pins. We are using SPI
(serial peripheral interface) for our encoders and our stepper motor drivers, and I2C
(inter-integrated circuit) for our compass. After last year, we realized the number of chip select
pins on the pico could be lessened by using a multiplexer, bringing the number of chip select
pins on the pico from four to three. To power the board and the relay, we have terminal blocks
that are fed 5 volts and 15 volts from the power distribution PCB.

Power Distribution PCB

Figure 11. Render of power distribution PCB
The new power distribution PCB contains buck converters that are now integrated into
the PCB instead of being on separate modules. By doing this, compared to last year's solutions
of having 5 separate modules attached via connectors to the main board, this solution takes up
less space and would also be more reliable. We are now using buck converters that are different
for each needed voltage. We still have the same general layout of a pair of 50V to 25V buck
converters that have an output that is fed to a connector, along with 3 more buck converters to
create 15V, 12VV, and 15V. Fuses are present for safety on each output, along with one on the
input. We are also now using connectors that allow for easier attachment of cables, so that we
can swap PCBs and the other components connected to it more easily, due to the cramped
environment that it will be placed in inside the boat. Additionally, the use of components
integrated into the PCB allows the overall size to be reduced compared to the versions from
prior years. This PCB will be mounted in the main PCB box alongside the digital PCB. This PCB
is always powered and does not communicate with the digital PCB. Compared to last year’s
version, the outputs and fuses are also labeled so that testing can be done without needing to
have documentation on hand to determine voltages on the outputs.

(inter-integrated circuit) for our compass. After last year, we realized the number of chip select
pins on the pico could be lessened by using a multiplexer, bringing the number of chip select
pins on the pico from four to three. To power the board and the relay, we have terminal blocks
that are fed 5 volts and 15 volts from the power distribution PCB.


Power Distribution PCB




                            Figure 11. Render of power distribution PCB

        The new power distribution PCB contains buck converters that are now integrated into
the PCB instead of being on separate modules. By doing this, compared to last year's solutions
of having 5 separate modules attached via connectors to the main board, this solution takes up
less space and would also be more reliable. We are now using buck converters that are different
for each needed voltage. We still have the same general layout of a pair of 50V to 25V buck
converters that have an output that is fed to a connector, along with 3 more buck converters to
create 15V, 12VV, and 15V. Fuses are present for safety on each output, along with one on the
input. We are also now using connectors that allow for easier attachment of cables, so that we
can swap PCBs and the other components connected to it more easily, due to the cramped
environment that it will be placed in inside the boat. Additionally, the use of components
integrated into the PCB allows the overall size to be reduced compared to the versions from
prior years. This PCB will be mounted in the main PCB box alongside the digital PCB. This PCB
is always powered and does not communicate with the digital PCB. Compared to last year’s
version, the outputs and fuses are also labeled so that testing can be done without needing to
have documentation on hand to determine voltages on the outputs.

Water Cooling

Figure 12. Layout of the water cooling system
The water cooling system was upgraded compared to last year due to the motor power
restrictions. We have increased our pump strength (both pressure and gallons per minute) and
the size of the reservoir. Our motor has two 3/16 inch outlets for the cooling liquid to pass
through. However, the inlet of the motor is essentially one quarter of the size ((3/8)^2/(3/16^2) =
4) of the pump outlet. Because of that, it was necessary to create a bypass loop between the
inlet and the outlet of the motor, so that the total area is preserved. A needle valve was added
as well to regulate the amount of water passing through the motor. The system can handle up to
60 PSI of pressure (as opposed to the expected 20 PSI), and can theoretically keep the water
under 40 degrees with the running motor.

Autopilot
AutoBoat at Virginia Tech is focused on creating a custom, open-source autopilot and
ground station application for motorboats and sailboats with advanced autonomy features from
scratch. Creating an autopilot from scratch allows us to have complete control over the
autopilot. With complete control, we are able to develop an autopilot that can be transferred to
different systems. Full control also allows us to implement more advanced autonomy features,
such as robust semantic collision avoidance and object detection, docking, COLREGs
compliance, and GPS denied navigation. Existing open source autopilots such as PX4 and
Ardupilot don’t have official support for these features. As we continue to develop our custom
autopilot, we plan to implement these more advanced features to further open source
development towards full autonomous navigation. The open source implementation of our
motorboat autopilot can be found here: https://github.com/autoboat-vt/autoboat_vt, and our
telemetry server can be found here: https://github.com/autoboat-vt/telemetry_server. Due to our

High-Level Autopilot Architecture
Our autopilot utilizes the robotic operating system (ROS) in order to facilitate efficient
and simple communication between our sensor drivers, the Raspberry Pi Pico that drives our
motors, and the autopilot via standardized message types.
ROS projects are structured as a system of nodes that are responsible for performing
logically distinct tasks asynchronously. These nodes communicate amongst each other by
exposing user-defined variables to named buses, colloquially referred to as “topics”. Figure 13
illustrates all of the different ROS nodes we created and their inputs and outputs sent via topics.

Figure 13. A diagram that shows how each of the ROS nodes in our autopilot system
communicates with each other.

Motorboat Simulation
The motorboat simulation was created from scratch using Gazebo Harmonic, an
open-source general-purpose physics simulator. The simulation has a boat with one rudder and
thruster that is controlled using Gazebo topics, which are translated to and from ROS topics to
facilitate control via the autopilot. In order to simulate realism, the simulation uses various
plugins to model hydrodynamic forces, lift, drag, rudder dynamics, and more. Some of these
plugins are from the Gazebo Harmonic project, and we created the rest. This simulation allows
us to validate and test our autopilot more robustly with realistic data, so that we only need to
fine-tune it for the real boat. In the future, we plan to add better modeling for waves and more

Computer Vision and Localization Algorithm Development
Our computer vision system was created from scratch and built off of industry-standard
vision frameworks and AI inference models. We use a framework called DeepStream, which
was built by NVIDIA to add on to Gstreamer, a popular open-source computer vision framework.
We use DeepStream and Gstreamer for two primary reasons: flexibility and performance.
GStreamer provides a modular pipeline that can achieve almost any functionality, and
DeepStream provides large performance benefits with its GPU integration. A GStreamer
pipeline consists of a series of plugins connected to each other, passing data down a pipeline.
DeepStream adds plugins for object-detection tasks like inference and tracking. The primary
plugins we use are camera input, AI inference, object tracking, and visualization. Our camera
plugin takes frames from an Intel RealSense D457 depth camera and passes the corresponding
tensors to the inference plugin. After inference, a tracking module assigns unique IDs to each
detected object. Finally, for visualization, we can save the images or display a video.
Inserting a probe into the pipeline allows us to access the bounding box results. These
raw bounding boxes are sent to the autopilot node for use in collision avoidance, but we can
also use them for triangulation. Using GPS and heading data, we can track how an object
moves relative to the boat and calculate its absolute position on the water. To triangulate an
object, we create a vector for each frame starting at the boat’s position and pointing in the
direction of the object. After enough detections, we can find where these vectors intersect, and
that is the position of the object. These triangulation results are sent to the autopilot node for
navigation.

To train our computer vision model, we synthesized our image data with public data to
create one central dataset stored on Roboflow, a software that allows us to use specialized
labeling and editing options needed for computer vision. After reviewing each image individually
to make sure the dataset correctly labels the objects within the environment, we used YOLO to
create a neural network from a single pass of the dataset. This avoids overfitting by having a
training algorithm that doesn’t reuse images, which helps predict images accurately even
outside of those on which the model has been trained. Fine-tuning the model parameters has
allowed us to accurately create bounding boxes of obstacles captured by the boat’s camera.

autopilot takes in the current rudder angle as an input and outputs the RPM of the propeller
motor as a decaying exponential function of the rudder angle, as shown in Equation 1. The min
rpm, max rpm, and k (decay rate) are all hyperparameters that can be changed from the ground
station. Turning at high speed may cause the boat to start to tip over, so this controller accounts
for a reduction in speed when turning.

Equation 1. Relates the current rudder angle to the rpm of the motorboat. The minimum rpm,

More advanced autonomy features, such as collision avoidance and avoiding “no-go”
zones, can then be built off of orchestrating waypoints in specific ways. In order to avoid “no-go”
zones on the map, which can represent small islands, the dock, or other boats, we simply
employ an A* algorithm to search for a path around these obstacles, and then place
intermediate waypoints along the desired path.
The A* algorithm works by calculating the cost of each direction the boat takes next. For
this application, we calculate the cost of 8 cardinal directions (north, east, south, west,
northeast, northwest, southeast, and southwest). The cost is a sum of the movement cost and
the heuristic cost. The movement cost is the cost of moving to the next position, and the
heuristic cost is a general rule for getting to the destination. Each new intermediate waypoint
generated counts as a movement cost of +1. For example, if the boat has to move to 5
intermediate waypoints to avoid collision, that is a total movement cost of 5. We use Euclidean
distance from the node at the end of each direction to our destination as our heuristic cost. For
example, if our destination is north of our position, the node north of our position will have the
least heuristic cost. The algorithm then generates a path that minimizes the cost, which results
in a path that both uses the fewest intermediate waypoints and is the most direct to our
destination.
We define a “nogo” zone as a group of nodes that are closed. When a node is closed, a
direction cannot be generated, so a path is not made to that node. With these constraints
defined, our A* algorithm will create the shortest direct path that successfully avoids all
obstacles.

Autopilot Failsafes and Safety Measures
In order to ensure that our autopilot does not act unpredictably whenever GPS loses
signal or if we somehow disconnect from our sensors, our custom autopilot employs several
failsafes. We use a radio remote controller to have remote control/ override in case the autopilot
is malfunctioning or is about to do something dangerous. By flicking a single toggle on the
remote controller, we can disable the autopilot and return to fully RC control to manually steer
the boat out of danger. If our remote controller receiver driver, GPS driver, and/ or compass
driver disconnects or stops broadcasting data at any point in time, then the autopilot will
automatically set the propeller motor rpm to 0 to avoid dangerous behaviour.

Telemetry Data and the Ground Station
To control and monitor our boat and autopilot from the shore, we created a ground
station using the PyQT framework and Leaflet JavaScript library. The ground station has been
significantly improved since last year, and now features a new set of tools to help users
effectively monitor and control the boat. An example screenshot of the program can be seen in
Appendix Figure 3.
The biggest addition to our telemetry was implementing the ability for the ground station
to switch between multiple simulations/ boats, so that we can control an entire fleet of boats at
the same time. We needed to add a SQLite database to store the boat data for each user, and
learn how to make it fast enough to be viable for rapid changes. In the long run, having this
database has made adding new features to our Flask telemetry server much easier, almost to
the point where it doesn’t require much thought. Additionally, it allows us to restart the telemetry
server without losing data.
The next big feature we implemented was the ability to fine tune the autopilot’s
parameters while it was running. We found that the best way to do this was to store each unique
autopilot parameter configuration on the telemetry server only if it was not already registered. In
order to determine whether the parameter configuration was unique, we hash the file and
compare it to our existing list of known hashes. This feature can be seen in Appendix Figures 4
and 5.
After looking at similar applications to our own, we thought that graphing the numerical
boat data fields would be a useful addition. We implemented this with a library called pyqtgraph,
due to its high performance and simplicity. We now have the ability to select which data fields
we would like to have graphed, while the boat is running. This has helped speed up debugging
of our PID controller, as it is often much easier to interpret a graph in comparison to a single
number. This feature can be seen in Appendix Figure 6.
Since it is fairly expensive to send data over LTE, we decided to shift our focus towards
optimizing the size of the packets sent from the telemetry node. Our current system first sends
an ordered list containing elements of the form (field_name, field_datatype) for each boat data
field. We then form a struct (in Python) containing the boat data and send the raw bytes over the
network. The telemetry server uses the ordering of the first list we sent to decode the struct back
into a dictionary, which can be easily interpreted by the ground station. The connection between
the ground station and telemetry server doesn’t use LTE, so we don’t have the same cost
restriction.
In the future, we plan on adding the ability to view a live camera feed from the boat,
complete with bounding boxes with image classification diagnostic information. In addition, we
would like for our Leaflet map to be more feature rich and visually descriptive of particular boat
data fields, such as the current rudder angle and the current velocity vector.
